sections.h: 2 Clement: sayings of Jesus in no Gospel
sections.b: The sermon called 2 Clement quotes the Lord about a dozen times, and several of the sayings are in no Gospel. In 4:5 the Lord warns that even those 'gathered with me in my embrace' will be thrown out if they do not keep his commandments. In 5:2-4 a saying close to Luke 10:3 ('like lambs surrounded by wolves') becomes a dialogue: Peter asks, 'But what if the wolves tear the lambs to pieces?', and Jesus answers that dead lambs need not fear wolves. In 8:5 words in no Gospel ('If you did not keep what is small, who will give you what is great?') are joined to Luke 16:10. Lake's note on 4:5 and 5:2-4: 'The source ... is unknown: it is often supposed to have been the Gospel of the Egyptians, but there is no clear evidence of this.' 13:2 has a 'woe' whose source, Lake says, 'is unknown'.
sections.refs: 2 Clement 4:5; 2 Clement 5:2-4; 2 Clement 8:5; 2 Clement 13:2; Luke 10:3; Luke 16:10

sections.b: Asked when his kingdom would come, the Lord answers: 'When the two are one, and the outside is like the inside, and the male with the female is neither male nor female' (2 Clement 12:2). Clement of Alexandria quotes nearly the same words as Julius Cassianus gave them, with an extra line ('When you trample on the garment of shame'), and says in his Greek, as Lightfoot prints it: 'In the four Gospels handed down to us we do not have the saying, but in the one according to the Egyptians' (Stromata 3.13). Cassianus used it against marriage; the preacher explains it as truthfulness, good works and purity between Christian men and women (12:3-5). Lake notes that an Oxyrhynchus papyrus published by Grenfell and Hunt seems to have a similar saying, and calls the relation between these texts 'still unsolved'.

uncommon: Lightfoot thought the preacher of 2 Clement used the Gospel of the Egyptians 'as authoritative, and apparently as his chief evangelical narrative'; Lake thought the evidence for this unclear.

sections.b: The sermon called 2 Clement quotes Isaiah 54:1 and goes on: 'And another Scripture also says, "I did not come to call righteous people. I came to call sinners"' (2 Clement 2:4), words found in Matthew 9:13 and Mark 2:17. George Reid's article on the canon in the Catholic Encyclopedia called it the place 'in which we find, for the first time after 2 Peter 3:16, the word Scripture applied to a New Testament book.' The same preacher names 'the Books and the apostles' together (14:2), which Lightfoot read as the Old Testament and the apostles' writings. 2 Clement itself was copied in Codex Alexandrinus, whose table of contents, Fenlon writes, includes it in the list of New Testament books; the Apostolic Canons (canon 85) name 'Two Epistles of Clemens' among the New Testament books, after Jude and before Acts; but Eusebius said the ancients made no use of it (Church History 3.38.4), and no church's Bible includes it today.

The sermon called 2 Clement answers people in the church who said 'that this flesh is not judged and does not rise' (2 Clement 9:1). Its argument is simple: you were saved and received your sight in this flesh, you were called in the flesh, and you will come to judgment in the flesh; Christ, who was spirit at first, 'became flesh', so 'we too will receive our reward in this flesh' (9:2-5). Lake names 'a belief in the resurrection of the flesh' as one of the sermon's three aims, and Lightfoot thought it the doctrine the preacher 'especially dwells' on. The same reasoning stands behind Paul's answer at Corinth (1 Corinthians 15:12-20).

In 2 Clement 'the flesh' is not the sinful nature but the body, which is to be kept 'pure' (8:4, 6) and guarded 'as a temple of God' (9:3). In chapter 14 the preacher builds a picture: the church is 'the body of Christ', the flesh is the 'copy' and the spirit the 'original', and 'whoever has abused the flesh has abused the church' (14:2-4). The flesh can share in 'life and incorruption' when the Holy Spirit is joined to it (14:5).

sections.h: The immortal fruit of the resurrection (2 Clement 19)
sections.b: The sermon called 2 Clement ends its appeal with a harvest: those who obey, 'even if they suffer hardship for a little while in this world, ... will gather in the immortal fruit of the resurrection', and the godly 'will live again above with the fathers' (2 Clement 19:3-4).

sections.h: Repent while you are on earth (2 Clement)
sections.b: Repentance is the word the sermon called 2 Clement repeats most: 'So while we are on earth, let us repent' (2 Clement 8:1). A potter can reshape a pot until it goes into the kiln, and 'after we have left the world, we can no longer confess our sins or repent there' (8:2-3). The preacher asks for repentance 'from a sincere heart' as the payment we owe God (9:8), 'now at last' (13:1), 'while we have time' (16:1), and confesses that he himself is 'a sinner through and through' (18:2).
sections.refs: 2 Clement 8:1-3; 2 Clement 9:7-8; 2 Clement 13:1; 2 Clement 16:1; 2 Clement 17:1; 2 Clement 18:2; 2 Clement 19:1

sections.b: The sermon called 2 Clement speaks of baptism as something received that must be kept: 'if we do not keep our baptism pure and unstained' (2 Clement 6:9), 'of those who have not kept the seal' (7:6), 'keep the flesh pure and the seal spotless' (8:6). 'The seal' (Greek sphragis) is baptism; Lake's English translates it 'the seal of baptism'. The preacher does not say what happens to someone who breaks the seal, but calls everyone to repent while there is time.

sections.h: The first church, the spiritual one (2 Clement 14)
sections.b: The sermon called 2 Clement speaks of 'the first church, the spiritual one, which was created before the sun and moon' (2 Clement 14:1). It joins Ephesians 1:23 ('the living church is the body of Christ') and Genesis 1:27 ('male and female': 'the male is Christ, the female is the church') to teach that the church existed from the beginning and 'was revealed in the flesh of Christ' (14:2-3). Lightfoot saw in it a step between Paul's teaching that God chose a people 'before the world was founded' (Ephesians 1:4) and the Valentinians' heavenly 'Church'. The sermon also reads the barren woman of Isaiah 54:1 as 'our church' (2:1).

sections.h: 'Almsgiving lightens the weight of sin' (2 Clement 16:4)
sections.b: The sermon called 2 Clement says: 'So almsgiving is good, as repentance for sin is. Fasting is better than prayer, but almsgiving is better than both. And "love lays a cover over a great number of sins," while prayer from a good conscience rescues from death ... almsgiving lightens the weight of sin' (2 Clement 16:4). It quotes 1 Peter 4:8 exactly and stands in the line of Tobit 12:8-9, but its ranking of fasting above prayer is its own. How the churches read such teaching is set out in the cards at Proverbs 16:6 and Tobit 4.

The sermon called 2 Clement ranks the three works of piety: 'Fasting is better than prayer, but almsgiving is better than both' (2 Clement 16:4). Jesus treats the three side by side (Matthew 6:1-18), and the Bible never sets prayer below fasting.

sections.h: The day of judgment in 2 Clement
sections.b: The sermon called 2 Clement begins with Christ 'the Judge of the living and the dead' (2 Clement 1:1) and returns to the judgment again and again: the day 'burning like an oven', when 'the secret and open deeds of people will be brought to light' (16:3); the unbelievers astonished to see 'the kingship of the world in Jesus' hands' (17:5); the righteous giving glory to God (17:7). Its point is always practical: repent now.

The sermon called 2 Clement quotes Isaiah 66:24 twice in the Greek Bible's form, 'they will be a spectacle to all flesh' (2 Clement 7:6; 17:5), of those who have not kept the seal of baptism and of the unbelievers at the judgment. It speaks of 'the fire of Gehenna' in a saying of Jesus (5:4), of 'eternal punishment' (6:7, as Matthew 25:46) and of 'a fire that is never put out' (17:7).
sections.refs: 2 Clement 5:4; 2 Clement 6:7; 2 Clement 7:6; 2 Clement 17:5-7; Isaiah 66:24; Mark 9:48

sections.b: The sermon called 2 Clement takes Malachi 4:1 ('the day is coming, burning like an oven') for 'the day of judgment', and adds from the Greek Isaiah 34:4 that 'some of the heavens will melt, and the whole earth will be like lead melting in the fire' (2 Clement 16:3).

The sermon called 2 Clement says that at the judgment 'some of the heavens will melt' (2 Clement 16:3). Lake's note: the text 'may be defended as a reference to the early Christian belief in seven concentric heavens surrounding the Earth', though Lightfoot proposed reading 'the powers of heaven'.

sections.h: The contest and the crown (2 Clement 7)
sections.b: The sermon called 2 Clement builds a whole chapter on the athletic games: many 'sail in' for contests that perish, only those who train hard are crowned, and a cheater 'is whipped, taken away and thrown out of the stadium' (2 Clement 7:1-4). Lightfoot, whose note on the whip names the officials of the games who used it, took the picture as a sign that the sermon was preached near the Isthmian games at Corinth. The picture returns at the end: 'We are competing in the trial of the living God' (20:2). These are Greek athletic contests, not the Roman shows, but the language of contest and crown is the same that Paul uses (1 Corinthians 9:24-27).

The sermon called 2 Clement reads the line of Isaiah 54:1 'cry aloud, you who have no labor pains' as a call to 'lift up our prayers to God with a single heart, and not lose heart' (2 Clement 2:2), promises that God answers 'while you are still speaking' (15:3, from Isaiah 58:9) and is 'more ready to give than the one who asks is to ask' (15:4), and says that 'prayer from a good conscience rescues from death' (16:4).

sections.h: A sermon after the reading (2 Clement 19:1)
sections.b: 'After the God of truth, I am reading you an appeal to pay attention to what is written' (2 Clement 19:1). Lightfoot read 'the God of truth' as God speaking in the Scripture just read, and compared Justin Martyr's account of Sunday worship, where 'the memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read' before the leader's teaching (First Apology 67). The sermon shows that order at work: reading first, then the sermon, read aloud from a written text. Lightfoot called it 'the first example of a Christian homily'.

sections.h: 2 Clement: a sermon under Clement's name
sections.b: The sermon known as 2 Clement names no author. It came to bear Clement's name because it was copied after 1 Clement in the manuscripts: Lightfoot thought both were kept together at Corinth and that 'in the course of transcription' the two came to seem 'of the same kind and by the same author'. Eusebius wrote that 'there is said to be a second epistle of Clement', but that the ancients made no use of it (Church History 3.38.4), and Jerome that it 'is rejected by earlier writers' (Lives of Illustrious Men 15). Lake: 'it cannot have been written by the author of I. Clement'.

The preacher of 2 Clement reminds his hearers that 'we bowed down to stones and wood, gold, silver and bronze, things people had made' (2 Clement 1:6), and that now 'we who are living do not sacrifice to dead gods' (3:1). The church had commandments 'to pull people away from idols and teach them' (17:1).

The sermon called 2 Clement warns against people who 'keep on teaching evil to innocent souls' and will face 'a double judgment, they and those who listen to them' (2 Clement 10:5). It does not name them. Lightfoot linked them with those who said 'this flesh is not judged and does not rise' (9:1), and saw an early, unnamed form of later Gnostic teaching.

The preacher of 2 Clement calls his whole sermon 'the advice I have given about self-control' (2 Clement 15:1). He means keeping the flesh pure (8:4-6), saying goodbye to the soul's pleasures (16:2), and purity between brothers and sisters (12:5). Lightfoot noted its 'Encratite tendencies', a leaning toward the strict self-denial of a later movement, though the sermon nowhere forbids marriage.

The sermon called 2 Clement mentions the church's leaders only as 'the elders' who warn the congregation (2 Clement 17:3) and 'told us about our salvation' (17:5). It names no overseer (bishop). Lightfoot thought the preacher was himself a church leader speaking as one of his hearers; Harnack, as Lightfoot reports him, thought him a layman.

The sermon called 2 Clement quotes Luke 16:13 ('No household slave can be a slave to two masters') and says this age and the next 'are two enemies' (2 Clement 6:1-5). It tells its hearers to treat the world's goods 'as belonging to someone else' (5:6), and answers the complaint that 'the wicked' grow rich: if God paid at once, 'we would be chasing profit and not godliness' (20:1-4).

The sermon called 2 Clement explains a saying from the Gospel of the Egyptians to mean that 'a brother who sees a sister should have no thought of her as female, and she should have no thought of him as male' (2 Clement 12:5). It is a rule of purity, not a ban on marriage; Clement of Alexandria reports that Julius Cassianus used the same saying against marriage (Stromata 3.13).

The sermon called 2 Clement opens: 'we must think of Jesus Christ as we think of God, as the Judge of the living and the dead' (2 Clement 1:1). It introduces a saying of Jesus with 'God says' (13:4) and says Christ 'was spirit at first and became flesh' (9:5). Lake names its 'high Christology' as one of its three aims.

sections.h: Spirit at first, then flesh (2 Clement 9:5)
sections.b: The sermon called 2 Clement argues from the incarnation to the resurrection of the body: 'If Christ, the Lord who saved us, was spirit at first and became flesh, and called us in that way, then we too will receive our reward in this flesh' (2 Clement 9:5). Lightfoot called it the pre-existence of the Son 'presented in a somewhat unusual form'; one manuscript (C) reads 'Word' for 'spirit', as in John 1:14.

sections.h: Leaving our stay as resident aliens (2 Clement 5)
sections.b: The sermon called 2 Clement turns the picture into a call to be ready to leave: 'let us leave behind our stay as resident aliens in this world, and do the will of the one who called us. Let us not be afraid to leave this world' (2 Clement 5:1). Our 'stay in this world, in this flesh, is small and brief' (2 Clement 5:5), so we should 'treat the things of this world as belonging to someone else' (2 Clement 5:6). The word is paroikia, the stay of a foreigner without citizen rights, as in 1 Peter 1:17. Where 1 Clement and Polycarp greet churches that live as resident aliens in their cities, this preacher makes the word a reason not to fear death or want this world's goods (2 Clement 5:2-7).
